extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and critics of humor and literary/theatrical theory; playwrights and comedians interested in the mechanics of the comic
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic criteria for what makes things comic: the essay explains the psychological, logical, and social conditions that produce laughter and comic effect, illustrated with literary and theatrical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional / specialised style as comic
rubrics_metrics.description: The ludicrous that springs from applying a specialised or professional vocabulary, manner, or strategy to ordinary affairs of life (professional habit expressed where ordinary speech is expected).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coarser when merely technical jargon is misapplied; more refined when it also reveals a peculiarity of character. Examples: Regnard's Joueur using gambling terms for personal names; Molière's Femmes savantes translating scientific ideas into feminine sensibility (e.g., 'Epicurus is charming').

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast of particular logic and universal (common-sense) logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic effects arise from the opposition between a logic valid within a particular circle (professional or group logic) and the universal/common-sense logic shared by the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrast produces special comic effects distinct from mere absurdity; recognize when a character's internal 'logic' is consistent within a closed system but contradicts external reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdity of a definite kind (not general absurdity)
rubrics_metrics.description: When absurdity appears in the comic it is a very special, definite kind: the comic infuses its own particular essence into the absurd, rather than the absurd being a general, undifferentiated contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Toying with generic absurdity will often fail to produce laughter unless it is of the particular kind Bergson isolates (e.g., grounded in rigidity or inversion of common sense). Craft comic situations so the absurdity reflects the cause (e.g., fixed idea, dream-logic) rather than being random.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion of common sense / imagination dominating perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic arises when one seeks to mould things on an internal idea instead of moulding ideas on things—seeing what one is thinking of rather than thinking of what one sees (Don Quixote example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a specific form of absurdity: a privileged recollection or idea dominates perception and forcibly imposes its form on external reality; develop characters whose imagination persistently misreads neutral stimuli as confirming their idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigidity, automatism, and obsessive one-idea behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: At the root of the comic is a sort of rigidity or automatism: a character follows one path or one idea obsessively, is absentminded, keeps strictly to one line and refuses to adapt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many comic scenes reduce to 'a character following up his one idea' despite interruptions. Use persistent, inflexible repetition of an idée fixe to elicit comic effect; contrast with normal adaptive common-sense to heighten laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dream-logic resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: The particular logic of the comic resembles the logic of dreams: partial use of recollections, substitution of ideas for perceptions, weakened tension of reasoning, and acceptance of counterfactual or implausible links.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic reasoning counterfeits true reasoning just enough to seem plausible to a mind 'dropping off to sleep.' Use truncated or superficially logical arguments, non sequiturs that mimic dream transitions, and reassignment of meaning (sound over sense) to provoke laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play upon words and superficial idea relations
rubrics_metrics.description: As relations between ideas grow more superficial, play upon ideas tends toward play upon words: the sound becomes more important than the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witticisms often take the form of abridged reasonings where only beginning and end are given; in performance, emphasize phonetic or surface parallels to exploit this tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and comic obsession
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurrent images, refrains, or burdens (the same phrase or image repeated with shifting interpretations) often produce a comic effect resembling dream obsessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition creates expectation and then displacement; employ repeated motifs that take on new, increasingly implausible meanings to mimic dream recurrence and elicit laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crescendo toward absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: A progressive sequence in which one concession to absurdity leads to another, each more serious, until a crowning absurdity is reached (a rising spiral of increasing extravagance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use incremental escalation—small absurdities that compound—to produce the peculiarly dreamlike sensation and eventual rousing (the audience's awakening at the play's absurd climax). Examples: some Molière plays (Monsieur de Pourceaugnac, Bourgeois gentilhomme).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fusion/confusion of identities (self and other)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dreamlike fusions where two persons become one yet remain distinct, or where the dreamer simultaneously is and is not himself; similar confusions can produce comic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit narrative or dialogic ambiguity in personhood or perspective (e.g., Mark Twain's reporter dialogue where the narrator both is and is not the twin) to create the strange, comic sensation of split identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relaxation / invitation to play (temporary sympathy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic induces a relaxation or lapse of intellectual tension that invites the audience to 'join in the game'—a fleeting sympathy where we momentarily adopt the comic character's gestures and thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fleeting identification relieves 'the strain of thinking' but is short-lived; structure comic moments to allow initial empathetic mirroring before the corrective element manifests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as corrective / social function (humiliation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter functions chiefly as society's corrective: it humiliates and intimidates those who transgress social norms or impertinences; it is not primarily benevolent and often hits indiscriminately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the punitive social dimension of laughter: comedic ridicule can improve social conformity but is apt to be unjust or unkind in particulars. When crafting satire or ridicule, balance corrective intent with ethical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic types as models of impertinence
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist predominant comic types (models of impertinence); intermediate varieties borrow comic quality from their resemblance to these prototypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the archetypal impertinences your piece echoes; much comic variety arises from resemblance to these central types rather than wholly novel mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter's mixed motive: spite, egoism, pessimism in the laugher
rubrics_metrics.description: Behind the laugher's apparent relaxation lies a spark of mischief or spite; laughter can enhance the laugher's self-assertion and conceit, revealing egoistic and sometimes pessimistic motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that audience laughter may reflect superiority and malice as much as delight; authors and performers should consider ethical dimensions of inviting laughter at others' expense.
